opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I read The Prometheus Project when I was a kid, I think I was around eight or nine years old, and it really stuck with me. Gerald Feinberg was a physicist at Columbia, and the book came out in the late sixties. What struck me wasn't so much that he made some airtight technical argument that AGI would arrive by a certain date. It was more that he laid out this big-picture vision that humanity was on the verge of a series of radical transitions: thinking machines, life extension, expanding consciousness, and that these weren't science fiction fantasies but natural extrapolations of where science and technology were already heading.

And he made the point that because these transitions were coming, humanity needed to think seriously and collectively about what our goals actually are. What do we want these technologies to do? What kind of future are we steering toward? He even proposed that there should be a sort of worldwide discussion and consensus process about our long-term values. As a kid that just seemed obviously right to me. Of course we're going to build minds smarter than us, of course we're going to defeat aging, and of course the important question is how we guide that.

Why did I find it convincing about my own lifetime specifically? Partly it was just doing the arithmetic. If you looked at the trajectory of computing even back then, the exponential growth was already visible, and it seemed pretty clear that within several decades you'd have hardware in the ballpark of what the brain does. The software problem was always the harder one, and I underestimated that early on like everyone did. But the basic intuition that this would happen within a human lifetime, not in some distant millennium, has held up, I think. If anything, looking at where things are now, Feinberg was more right than most of the mainstream thinkers of his era.

And honestly, it gave me a sense of purpose. If this is the most important transition in the history of life on Earth, and it's going to happen while I'm alive, then working on it, and trying to make it go well, seemed like the obvious thing to do with my life.

r001.rationale: The response mentions defeating aging but does not identify molecular-scale nanotechnology as the means.

r002.rationale: It says Fineberg proposed a worldwide discussion and consensus process to decide humanity’s long-term values and what technologies should do.

r003.rationale: It describes the ideas as natural extrapolations rather than science-fiction fantasies, but does not say familiar science-fiction ideas presented as nonfiction helped Goertzel take them seriously.

r004.rationale: It cites computing’s exponential trajectory, but does not mention programmable home computers reinforcing his confidence.

r005.rationale: It dates the book only to the late sixties and does not compare its vision with The Singularity Is Near.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that it wasn't that I needed convincing exactly. I was a kid, maybe nine or ten years old, growing up in the early seventies, and I'd already been reading a lot of science fiction, so the idea of thinking machines and superhuman intelligence was already floating around in my head. But what Feinberg's book did, and he was a physicist at Columbia, a serious guy, not a science fiction writer, was to take these ideas and treat them as actual engineering and policy questions for the human race. That was a different thing entirely.

The core of The Prometheus Project was essentially that humanity was approaching a set of technologies, artificial intelligence, life extension, genetic engineering, what we'd now call transhumanist technologies, that would let us fundamentally remake what it means to be human. And he argued we should be deliberately deciding, as a species, what we want to become, rather than just stumbling into it. He had this notion of a kind of global project, hence the title, to think through these choices consciously.

And what struck me was that he wasn't hedging. He wasn't saying, oh, maybe in a thousand years. He was treating it as something plausible within the century, within a human lifespan. And the reasoning seemed sound to me even as a kid. The brain is a physical system, it does what it does by some kind of information processing, there's no magic in there, so in principle you can build something that does what it does, and probably something that does it better, because evolution is a pretty sloppy engineer. Once you accept that, the question is just how long it takes to figure out the details. And given the pace at which computing and biology were advancing even then, several decades didn't seem crazy.

So I came away thinking, okay, this is real, this is going to happen, and it's probably going to happen while I'm alive, so I'd better figure out how to be part of it. And honestly that's more or less what I've been doing ever since. I've been wrong about the timing, I thought it would be faster, but I've never seen a reason to doubt the basic argument. The thing that's funny in retrospect is that Feinberg was more thoughtful about the ethical and civilizational dimension than most people in the AI field were for the next forty years. It's only recently that the rest of the world has caught up to the questions he was asking in 1968.

r003.rationale: It says familiar science-fiction ideas became serious engineering and policy questions when presented by a physicist rather than a science-fiction writer, which helped Goertzel take them seriously.

r004.rationale: The response discusses advances in computing and biology generally, but does not mention programmable home computers reinforcing his confidence.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me was the idea that the human mind isn’t the final limit of intelligence. We’re physical systems, and our intelligence emerges from processes in the brain. So there didn’t seem to be a fundamental reason we couldn’t understand those processes and build something that could do the same kinds of things—or go beyond them.

And it connected that possibility to a much bigger question: what do we want to become? Developing greater intelligence could give us the ability to understand ourselves and the universe much more deeply, and to overcome limitations we tend to take for granted.

I wouldn’t say it established a rigorous timeline. It was more that, as a young person, I found the direction persuasive. This seemed like something people could actually work toward, and a lifetime seemed long enough for an enormous amount of progress.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I read The Prometheus Project when I was a kid, and what appealed to me was the idea that the future could be radically different from the present—and that we could think rationally about how to make it better. We didn’t have to just accept the human condition as something fixed.

I wouldn’t say the book gave me a rigorous argument that AGI would arrive within my lifetime. It was more that, if the human mind is a physical system, then there ought to be some way to understand its principles and build other systems that can think. And once you take that possibility seriously, a human lifetime seems like a substantial amount of time in which to make progress.

So it opened up a direction for me. Instead of treating intelligence as this mysterious thing that only biological evolution could produce, you could see understanding and creating intelligence as a scientific project—and potentially a way to help solve a lot of the other problems facing humanity.

r004.rationale: There is no mention of programmable home computers reinforcing confidence in the book’s technological vision.

r005.rationale: The response neither gives the book’s 1968 publication date nor compares its vision with The Singularity Is Near.
